items.title: Ed Polcer interviewed by Monk Rowe, Tarrytown, New York, October 31, 1998
items.q: the shake or the wobble that I have as a part of my style was really out of Louis, I mean from listening out of Louis and from listening to Louis.

ctx.x: You must have occasion where you try to explain the differences — what there are — between New Orleans Dixieland, Chicago jazz and New York swing as you called it. Can you explain it to me? © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

Well no. How much tape do you have here? It would take quite a while. And again it’s the critics that put the handles on it. A player goes and plays, right? I consider the music I’m playing right now current. I’m playing music of today. For me it’s music of today. It’s the music that I hear. It’s like a composer or a painter. He can paint the way he feels. But I mean traditional, real New Orleans, was a lot of ensemble playing. Aside from Louis Armstrong, who grew out of that with solos, it was almost entire…
It was a good answer. When it came down to making a living when you were a young man, you were going to take a crack at being a full time musician.
